opus-5.5.text:
Because in the end, everything in AI comes back to people. Algorithms change, models change, and the compute you buy today is outdated in a few years. But the people you train carry the field forward for decades. A university's comparative advantage isn't building the biggest model; industry has far more money and compute. Our unique role is to cultivate the next generation: people who understand the fundamentals deeply and can define new problems, not just solve the ones handed to them.

I've worked in both industry and academia, and I've seen that the breakthroughs that matter most usually come from a small number of exceptional, well-trained people with the freedom to explore. Many of the people leading AI labs and companies today came out of university programs a decade or two ago. That's the real return on investment.

There's also the question of what kind of talent AI now requires. It's no longer enough to be a strong engineer. You need people who are interdisciplinary, who can bring AI into biology, healthcare, materials, and transportation, and who understand the responsibility that comes with the technology. Safety, ethics, and governance aren't side topics anymore. Universities are the natural place to form that kind of well-rounded person, with technical depth, breadth across fields, and a sense of values.

So when I say talent comes first, I don't mean research or industry collaboration is less important. Good research is how you train people, and real-world problems from industry are how you keep that training relevant. But the core product of a university is people. If we get that right, the research and the impact follow.

r001.rationale: The response says universities cultivate future leaders of AI labs and companies, but does not identify preparing future company CTOs as a goal.

r002.rationale: It calls people the university’s core product and says that if talent cultivation succeeds, research and impact follow.

r003.rationale: The response makes no comparison between China and the United States on technology leaders capable of architecting large systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Because a university’s most lasting output is people, not papers or products. Technology has cycles — a specific model, a specific chip, a specific application will be superseded in a few years. But a person trained well will be creating value for forty or fifty years, through several of those cycles.

When I came back to Tsinghua to build the AIR institute, I thought about this very carefully. Industry has far more computing power than any university, far more data, and in many cases higher salaries. If a university tries to compete with companies on training the largest models, it will lose, and it should lose — that is not its comparative advantage. What a university can do better than anyone is bring together young people with curiosity, give them real problems, surround them with mentors who have actually built things, and let them grow. Those people then go out — some to industry, some to start companies, some to stay in research — and that is how the ecosystem gets built.

There is also a timing issue. AI is at a point where the gap between what the field needs and the number of people who can really do it is enormous. Everybody talks about the shortage of GPUs, but the deeper shortage is talent — people who understand both the fundamentals and how to apply them to real domains like autonomous driving, biology, robotics. You cannot buy your way out of that shortage. You have to cultivate it, and that takes years, so you have to start early.

And frankly, it changes how you do research as well. If talent is the first goal, then you choose problems that are hard enough to stretch students, you insist on open publication and open-source so they build reputation and connections, and you resist the temptation to turn a lab into a contract shop. Research output then comes naturally — good people doing meaningful problems will produce good results. But if you reverse the order and optimize for output first, you often end up with neither.

r001.rationale: The response says some graduates may start companies, but does not identify preparing future company CTOs as a goal.

r002.rationale: It presents talented people as the lasting output and says strong research results follow from good people working on meaningful problems.

r003.rationale: It discusses a talent shortage broadly but makes no comparison between China and the United States on technology leaders able to architect large systems.

astra-6.text:
Because a university’s most lasting contribution to AI is the people it educates. Technologies change quickly, so we need to give students more than proficiency with today’s tools. We need to help them build strong foundations, ask good questions, think independently, and keep learning.

AI also reaches far beyond computer science. Students need opportunities to work across disciplines and understand the human consequences of what they build. If we cultivate people who combine technical ability with curiosity and responsibility, they will drive both the research and the applications. That is why I put talent cultivation first.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a university’s most lasting contribution to AI is the people it educates. Technologies change very quickly, so we shouldn’t simply train students to use today’s tools. We need to give them strong foundations, the ability to think independently, and the curiosity to explore problems we haven’t yet solved.

AI also reaches across disciplines. Students need opportunities to connect computing with science, engineering, medicine, and the humanities, and to understand the responsibility that comes with building these systems. If we cultivate people who can keep learning, ask important questions, and exercise good judgment, research and innovation will follow. That is why I put talent cultivation first.
